title: G R Balasubramaniam: Left School at 13, Built a Rs 1,000 Crore Dairy Empire
excerpt: From Rs 3,000 in savings and door-to-door butter deliveries in Bengaluru to GRB Dairy Foods' Rs 1,084 crore in annual revenue — the five-decade rise of G R Balasubramaniam.
body:
• G R Balasubramaniam left school at 13, moved from his Tamil Nadu village to Bengaluru in 1970, and spent 14 years learning the butter trade with his sister and brother-in-law.
  • In 1984, with Rs 6,000 in savings, he started selling butter door-to-door — about 75 kg a month — before expanding into ghee for hotels, sweet shops and households.
  • GRB Dairy Foods, built under his initials, set up its first factory in Bengaluru in 1991 and later expanded to Dindigul and Hosur, with the Chennai market added under the Udhayam brand in 1993.
  • The company reported revenue of more than Rs 1,084 crore in FY25, sells in over 40 countries including Singapore, Australia and the UAE, and employs around 2,500 people.

A 13-Year-Old in Bengaluru

G R Balasubramaniam was 13 when he left Class 8 in 1970 and moved from his village in Tamil Nadu to Bengaluru. He joined the butter business run by his elder sister and brother-in-law, and for the next 14 years he learned the trade from the ground up: buying butter from small producers, delivering it to customers, keeping the accounts, and learning how butter could be turned into ghee, according to YourStory, as reported by NDTV.

"I had no other option. My father could not take me back. So I told myself, this is my life now. And because I threw myself into it fully, I learned everything."

— G R Balasubramaniam, founder of GRB Dairy Foods

"That involvement for those 14 years is the reason I am where I am today," he said. When he married in 1984 at 28, he decided, six months later, to strike out on his own. His savings stood at Rs 6,000 — and Rs 3,000 of that went as advance rent on a small room.

Rs 3,000 and a Chit Fund

"I sat not knowing what to do. I knew butter, I knew ghee, but I had never been the one making decisions. It felt like a blank. Like nothing was there," Balasubramaniam recalled. His first move was to organize a chit fund to raise capital, and he used about Rs 50,000 from it to buy his first stock of butter.

He sold roughly 75 kg of butter every month, delivering it door-to-door across Bengaluru himself. Then he made the decision that changed everything: instead of selling only butter, he began converting it into ghee and supplying hotels, sweet shops and households. Within a year, his monthly income reached around Rs 25,000. He rented a 10-by-20-foot shop, hired a few workers, and began selling ghee under the initials G.R.B.

From Shop to Factories

GRB set up its first factory in Bengaluru in 1991, entered the Chennai market under the Udhayam brand in 1993, and added facilities in Dindigul and a larger factory in Hosur in 1999. The company spread across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, and eventually into international markets.

Today, GRB Dairy Foods sells ghee, sweets, snacks, spices and other products in more than 40 countries, including Singapore, Australia and the UAE — markets with large Indian diaspora communities that keep ghee on their shopping lists. Ghee remains the company's biggest business, contributing around 75 to 80 percent of total sales. GRB reported revenue of more than Rs 1,084 crore in FY25, is targeting around Rs 1,400 crore, and employs roughly 2,500 people.

The Arithmetic of Persistence

Balasubramaniam's story is often filed under inspiration, but it reads better as arithmetic. Fourteen years of apprenticeship before ownership. One pivot from butter to ghee. Factories added only when demand demanded them. The Rs 1,000 crore figure is the headline; the discipline is the story — a reminder, for diaspora entrepreneurs as much as anyone, that scale is usually the last chapter, not the first.
